Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-english-main-0-polish-long-0096", "row_sha256": "3dbd51b8348b970d4f79e18235ea2802612ab1e8bb4aa4b691087d76b23c0f71", "mode": "/polish", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Rewrite awkward phrasing into readable prose for the supplied profile, or plain prose when none is supplied. Preserve intent and certainty. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "
last saturday, april 13, the maple row seed exchange used the community room at the public library from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. this was the third year the exchange had been held there, and nia patel coordinated the day with six volunteers. the library room was available without a rental fee, but the group had to finish clearing the tables by 1:30, before the afternoon computer class came in. forty-two households signed the attendance sheet, including seventeen people who had not attended before. some visitors stayed for most of the four hours, while others picked up packets and left after a few minutes. the count was a count of households, not of individual people, because families often arrived together.

visitors brought 286 seed packets for the exchange. volunteers counted 214 as labeled well enough for the public tables, with a crop name and a year or season shown on the packet or on a note attached to it. another 63 packets had some useful information but lacked a date, had a label that could not be read, or had a mixture of seeds that was not clear. those went into a separate review box and were not placed on the tables during the event. nine packets were wet or visibly damaged and were kept off the exchange tables; the intake sheet did not record whether those packets were later discarded or taken home. the counts came from the intake tally and were not a count of seeds inside each packet.

rather than sort every packet by the garden where it came from, the volunteers arranged the public tables by crop group: beans and peas, other vegetables, herbs, flowers, and plants for pollinators. they put the labels facing up and left a small space between groups because people were stopping to read the packet notes. there were fewer herb packets than last year, according to the comparison written in the planning notebook, though no total from last year was copied into this year's intake sheet. tomato and bean packets drew the most questions at the tables. that was an observation by the volunteers, not a record of how many packets each visitor took.

at the entrance, nia asked new visitors to write down the name of a crop they hoped to grow this season. the sheet was optional, and 29 visitors added a crop name. tomatoes appeared nine times, beans five times, and lettuce four times; the remaining names appeared once or twice. one visitor left a blank line after writing “something my kids can water without a fuss.” nia said the list was useful for choosing what to ask people about, but it should not be treated as a survey of every household in maple row. visitors who did not fill in the sheet were not asked to explain why.

one volunteer, marcus lee, said, “people seemed more comfortable asking what the label meant when we left the packets on the table long enough to read together.” he had helped at the exchange in both earlier years. volunteers noted that visitors asked about planting depth, whether seeds could be started in pots, and how long saved seed might still germinate. they answered when they knew, and referred questions about particular varieties to the information printed on the packet. no one tested germination at the exchange, and the group did not give a guarantee about how any packet would grow. several visitors also compared notes about balcony containers, but the intake form did not collect information about where people planned to plant.

1. next exchange notes
- keep the crop-group signs, but make the lettering larger; two visitors asked where the flower table began.
- bring more blank labels and pencils. the supply was almost gone by 11:30, and one volunteer borrowed a marker from the library desk.
- ask donors to include a year on packets when they know it. volunteers should still keep unclear packets separate rather than guess at a date or crop.
- check whether the room can be booked until 2 p.m. next time. the tables were cleared by 1:26, but the last visitors were still talking near the door as the computer class arrived.

these points were copied from the volunteer debrief, and they are requests for planning, not changes already approved by the library. the group has not set a date for another exchange. nia said she would ask the library about its spring calendar before sharing a date publicly. no one volunteered to take over room booking, so she will contact the library again if the group decides to hold another event. the volunteers left the remaining packets in labeled boxes, with the review box separate from packets that had been available to visitors.

after the room was cleared, two volunteers checked the intake tally against the number of packets still in the labeled boxes. they found a difference of three packets, and the sheet does not explain whether those were handed out, moved between boxes, or counted twice. they left the recorded totals unchanged and wrote the difference in the margin for follow-up. the review box stayed closed during that check, so its contents were not recounted. the attendance sheet and crop-interest sheet were placed in the exchange folder, separate from the packet tally.

the assessment in the debrief was limited to the event itself: the exchange brought 42 households to the library room, and visitors used the tables and asked questions during the four-hour session. this assessment is based on the attendance sheet, intake tally, and volunteers' notes; it does not measure planting, germination, later seed sharing, or interest among people who did not attend. the unclear and damaged packets, the three-packet tally difference, and the optional crop-interest sheet limit what the records can establish about the seeds offered or what households wanted. the records support describing this event and its attendees, but they do not establish that seed access improved across maple row or that the same attendance would occur at another exchange.", "output": "Last Saturday, April 13, the Maple Row Seed Exchange used the community room at the public library from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. This was the third year the exchange had been held there, and Nia Patel coordinated the day with six volunteers. The library room was available without a rental fee, but the group had to finish clearing the tables by 1:30, before the afternoon computer class arrived. Forty-two households signed the attendance sheet, including seventeen people who had not attended before. Some visitors stayed for most of the four hours, while others picked up packets and left after a few minutes. The count was of households, not individuals, because families often arrived together.

Visitors brought 286 seed packets to the exchange. Volunteers counted 214 as sufficiently labeled for the public tables, with a crop name and a year or season shown on the packet or on an attached note. Another 63 packets had some useful information but lacked a date, had an illegible label, or contained a mixture of seeds that was unclear. Those packets went into a separate review box and were not placed on the tables during the event. Nine packets were wet or visibly damaged and were kept off the exchange tables; the intake sheet did not record whether they were later discarded or taken home. The counts came from the intake tally and did not represent the number of seeds inside each packet.

Rather than sorting each packet by the garden it came from, volunteers arranged the public tables by crop group: beans and peas, other vegetables, herbs, flowers, and plants for pollinators. They placed the labels face up and left a small space between groups because people stopped to read the packet notes. According to a comparison in the planning notebook, there were fewer herb packets than last year, although no total from last year was copied into this year’s intake sheet. Tomato and bean packets drew the most questions at the tables. This was an observation by the volunteers, not a record of how many packets each visitor took.

At the entrance, Nia asked new visitors to write down the name of a crop they hoped to grow this season. The sheet was optional, and 29 visitors added a crop name. Tomatoes appeared nine times, beans five times, and lettuce four times; the remaining names appeared once or twice. One visitor left a blank line after writing, “something my kids can water without a fuss.” Nia said the list was useful for choosing what to ask people about, but it should not be treated as a survey of every household in Maple Row. Visitors who did not fill in the sheet were not asked to explain why.

One volunteer, Marcus Lee, said, “People seemed more comfortable asking what the label meant when we left the packets on the table long enough to read together.” He had helped at the exchange in both earlier years. Volunteers noted that visitors asked about planting depth, whether seeds could be started in pots, and how long saved seed might still germinate. They answered when they knew and referred questions about particular varieties to the information printed on the packet. No one tested germination at the exchange, and the group did not guarantee how any packet would grow. Several visitors also compared notes about balcony containers, but the intake form did not collect information about where people planned to plant.

1. Next exchange notes
- Keep the crop-group signs, but make the lettering larger; two visitors asked where the flower table began.
- Bring more blank labels and pencils. The supply was almost gone by 11:30, and one volunteer borrowed a marker from the library desk.
- Ask donors to include a year on packets when they know it. Volunteers should still keep unclear packets separate rather than guess at a date or crop.
- Check whether the room can be booked until 2 p.m. next time. The tables were cleared by 1:26, but the last visitors were still talking near the door as the computer class arrived.

These points were copied from the volunteer debrief. They are requests for planning, not changes already approved by the library. The group has not set a date for another exchange. Nia said she would ask the library about its spring calendar before sharing a date publicly. No one volunteered to take over room booking, so she will contact the library again if the group decides to hold another event. The volunteers left the remaining packets in labeled boxes, with the review box separate from the packets that had been available to visitors.

After the room was cleared, two volunteers checked the intake tally against the number of packets still in the labeled boxes. They found a difference of three packets, and the sheet does not explain whether those packets were handed out, moved between boxes, or counted twice. They left the recorded totals unchanged and wrote the difference in the margin for follow-up. The review box remained closed during the check, so its contents were not recounted. The attendance sheet and crop-interest sheet were placed in the exchange folder, separate from the packet tally.

The debrief’s assessment was limited to the event itself: the exchange brought 42 households to the library room, and visitors used the tables and asked questions during the four-hour session. This assessment is based on the attendance sheet, intake tally, and volunteers’ notes; it does not measure planting, germination, later seed sharing, or interest among people who did not attend. The unclear and damaged packets, the three-packet tally difference, and the optional crop-interest sheet limit what the records can establish about the seeds offered or what households wanted. The records support describing this event and its attendees, but they do not establish that seed access improved across Maple Row or that the same attendance would occur at another exchange."}]
